newsitem.title: USA: Calif county welfare costs less than feared - report.
newsitem.headline: Calif county welfare costs less than feared - report.

text.p: Federal welfare reform's immigrant restrictions will cost California counties substantially less than what some had feared, according to a new state report.
The annual statewide cost for county general assistance programs could increase by up to $500 million, California's Legislative Analyst said in the report.
The $500 million estimate represents the worst-case scenerio, said Dan Rabovsky, who prepared the report.

"We think the impact will be significantly less (than $500 million), particularly because we expect many of them (immigrants) to attain citizenship, and secondarily because some of them will not seek GA (general assistance) for various reasons," Rabovsky said.

The California State Association of Counties had estimated that annual costs for general assistance -- currently about $450 million -- could balloon to as much as $1.3 billion, placing a heavy additional burden on the strained financial resources of counties.
County general assistance programs provide a minimum level of support, typically to single adult males who do not qualify for other types of assistance.
A provision in the new federal welfare legislation prohibits most legal immigrants who are non-citizens from receiving benefits under the Supplemental Security Income/State Supplementary Program.
About 200,000 legal immigrants currently receive these benefits in California could lose those benefits by August 1997 and potentially become eligible for county general assistance grants.

"Although the effects may not be nearly as large as initially feared, counties still could face additional costs related to the immigrant restrictions in welfare reform," the Legisaltive Analyst said in the report.

In California, distribution of the general assistance caseload is uneven. Los Angeles County has 35 percent of the state's population and 59 percent of the general assistance caseload. Los Angeles, San Francisco and Alameda counties have three-quarters of the state's general assistance caseload, according to the Legislative Analyst.
